title: Dive Deep Before Turning Back

concept.title: Depth-first search goes as deep as it can, then backs up; a stack does it without recursion
body: *Depth-first search* (DFS) explores one road to its end before trying another: from the current node it goes to an **unvisited neighbour**, and from there to an unvisited neighbour of that one, and so on; when a node has no unvisited neighbour left, the search **backs up** to the previous node. It is the natural way to explore a maze, and it is the basis of many algorithms (cycles, components, topological order).

The usual way to write it is a recursive function, but in a graph that is a path of 20000 nodes the recursion is 20000 calls deep, which fails in Python. The same order can be produced with an **explicit stack**: pop a node; if it was seen already, skip it; otherwise mark it, visit it, and push its neighbours. To make the smallest neighbour come out first, push the neighbours in **decreasing** order (the last pushed is the first popped).

body.code:
for lst in adj:
    lst.sort()
seen = [False] * (n + 1)
stack = [1]
order = []
while stack:
    v = stack.pop()
    if seen[v]:
        continue                       # it was reached by a shorter way meanwhile
    seen[v] = True
    order.append(v)
    for w in reversed(adj[v]):         # the smallest neighbour is pushed last, so it comes first
        if not seen[w]:
            stack.append(w)

body: The nodes are marked as seen **when they are popped**, not when they are pushed, because a node may be pushed several times by different neighbours; only its first pop counts. The order produced is exactly the order of the recursive version. The time is O(n + m).

statement: An undirected graph has `n` nodes and `m` edges. Do a depth-first search from node 1: from the current node go to its smallest unvisited neighbour; when there is none, go back to the node you came from. Print the nodes in the order in which they are first visited (only the nodes that can be reached from node 1).
inputFormat: The first line has `n` and `m`: the number of nodes (numbered 1 to n) and the number of edges.
Each of the next `m` lines has two numbers `u` and `v`: an edge between the nodes `u` and `v`.
outputFormat: The visited nodes in order on one line.
constraints: There are no self-loops and no repeated edges.

examples.note: From 1 go to 2, then to 5, then to 4, then to 3; node 6 is not reachable: 1 2 5 4 3.

hints: Use a stack; pop a node, skip it if it was seen, otherwise visit it and push its unseen neighbours.
Push the neighbours from the largest to the smallest, so that the smallest is popped first.

explanation: An explicit stack replaces the recursion: a node is visited when it is first popped, and its unseen neighbours are pushed from the largest to the smallest so that the smallest comes out first.
solution.complexity: Time O(n + m log m), space O(n + m).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n, m = map(int, input().split())
edges = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(m)]

adj = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
for u, v in edges:
    adj[u].append(v)
    adj[v].append(u)
for lst in adj:
    lst.sort()
seen = [False] * (n + 1)
stack = [1]
order = []
while stack:
    v = stack.pop()
    if seen[v]:
        continue
    seen[v] = True
    order.append(v)
    for w in reversed(adj[v]):
        if not seen[w]:
            stack.append(w)
print(*order)
